title: The less I knew, the surer I was.
dek: Students in the bottom quarter scored at the 12th percentile and guessed they were at the 62nd. Why the knowledge you need to do something is the same knowledge you need to see you did it badly.
whyThisIdea: Toate ideile rămase în backlog sunt marcate ca prea apropiate de articole publicate, iar ultimele cinci propuneri au fost toate despre bani și Black Friday, așa că am adăugat o idee nouă despre studiu și încredere: efectul Dunning-Kruger (Kruger & Dunning 1999 - cei din ultimul sfert erau la percentila 12 și credeau că sunt la 62), cu o contra-argumentare cinstită despre versiunea exagerată de pe internet.

entry.title: The less I knew, the surer I was.
entry.titleHtml: The less I knew, the surer I was.
entry.dek: Students in the bottom quarter scored at the 12th percentile and guessed they were at the 62nd. Why the knowledge you need to do something is the same knowledge you need to see you did it badly.
body: “Ignorance more frequently begets confidence than does knowledge.” — Charles Darwin

Have you ever asked yourself why the people who know the least about something are so often the most sure about it? Today is Saturday, the 28th of November, and it has been 73 days since the first article went up on this site. Last week I read my first articles again, and I noticed something I did not like. The less I knew about a subject, the faster I wrote about it. The things I really studied took me days, because every sentence had a “but”. So the question is: is confidence a measurement of what you know, or is it something completely different? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at is called the Dunning-Kruger effect, and I met it like most people do, as a joke on the internet - a graph with a big peak at the beginning and a funny name written on top of it. But behind the joke there is a real paper. In 1999, Justin Kruger and David Dunning, two psychologists at Cornell University, published it with a very long and very honest title: “Unskilled and unaware of it: How difficulties in recognizing one’s own incompetence lead to inflated self-assessments”. They gave Cornell students tests in humour, logical reasoning and grammar, and then they asked them one more question: how well do you think you did, compared to the others?

Firstly, let’s split the title in two, the way I like to do. “Unskilled” and “unaware of it”. Being unskilled is normal - everybody is unskilled at almost everything (I cannot play the violin, and I know it very well). The interesting half is the second one. Their idea is that for a lot of skills, the knowledge you need to do the thing is the same knowledge you need to judge if you did it well. If you do not know a grammar rule, you also cannot see that you broke it. If you do not understand a logic problem, your wrong answer looks exactly as good to you as the right one. <u>The same gap that makes you wrong also hides from you that you are wrong.</u> So this is not a problem of being stupid. It is a problem of not having the tool to check.

Secondly, the numbers, because this is the part that surprised me. The students who scored in the bottom quarter were, on average, at the 12th percentile - which means that 88% of the people did better than them. But when they were asked where they think they are, they put themselves at the 62nd percentile, above average.
Where they were: 12th percentile
Where they thought they were: 62nd percentile
That is a gap of 50 percentile points, half of the whole scale, and they did not feel any of it.

And it is not only Cornell students and grammar tests. In 1981, a psychologist named Ola Svenson asked groups of students in the USA and in Sweden, all of them drivers, to compare their driving skill with the other people in the same group. 93% of the American group and 69% of the Swedish group put themselves in the better half. Let’s put it a little bit in perspective with a class of 30 students, all different. By definition, only 15 of them can be in the better half. If 93% think they are, that is 30 × 0.93 = 27.9, so about 28 people.
People who think they are in the better half: 28
Places in the better half: 15
So at least 13 of those 28 are wrong, which is 46% of them. Almost half of the confident people cannot be right, and the maths does not even need to know who they are.

Thirdly, and this is the counter-case I have to be fair to, because the internet version of this effect is much stronger than the real one. The famous graph with the big peak is not in the paper. In the study, the students at the bottom still rated themselves lower than the students at the top did - they just rated themselves much too high. And the best students actually put themselves lower than they really were, because they thought the test was easy for everybody. On top of that, in 2016 a group of researchers led by Edward Nuhfer argued that part of the famous pattern appears even with random numbers, because of the way this kind of data is put into a graph. I am not able to judge those statistics myself (yes, I see the irony). But I think the fair version is this: almost everybody thinks they are a bit above average, and the people at the bottom simply have the longest way to fall.

So here is what I am going to try, because an article about overconfidence is worthless if I am confident I do not have it. Before every exam this winter, I write down the grade I think I will get, and after the results I write the real one next to it. Not to feel bad, but because I have never once compared the two, and I think the difference will tell me more about myself than any test. And for this blog, before I start an article I write how sure I am, from 1 to 10, that the main idea is right, and I write it again after I checked every number. If the second number is always higher, I am probably not checking hard enough.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I like this idea because it is not an insult to other people - it is about everyone, and that includes me. I am a student explaining psychology research on a personal blog, so I am exactly the kind of person this article is about. But I don’t enjoy what the internet did with it. “Dunning-Kruger” became a word you throw at somebody in an argument to say “you are stupid”, and being so sure that the other person is on the peak is, in a way, the effect itself. And I have to be honest about one more thing. A little bit of too much confidence is what makes people start. If I had known in September how much there is to know about habits or money, maybe I would never have written the first article. In my review of “Atomic Habits” I wrote that it was hard breaking that first layer, and maybe I only broke it because I did not know how thick it was. What I take from it is simple: confidence is how you feel, not what you know - so check the second one before you trust the first.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“Ignorance more frequently begets confidence than does knowledge.” — Charles Darwin
